prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, and the experimental realization of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I keep topological insulators (B016) as my preferred final configuration, with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. The round-1 exchange did not weaken the scientific case. The Kane-Mele Z2 invariant and quantum spin Hall state introduced a new classification of time-reversal-invariant insulators, and the HgTe edge-transport experiment tested that prediction directly. Olsson rightly pointed out that the strongest later confirmation is in three-dimensional materials, and that the HgTe transport data carry sample-quality subtleties. I therefore tighten the citation to the prediction and the HgTe realization of the quantum spin Hall state and avoid any wording that claims the whole field of topological matter. The 2016 prize concerned topological phase transitions and the Thouless-Haldane-Kosterlitz lineage; as Olsson argued, the Z2 classification is a distinct discovery, and Danielsson and Johansson's overlap worry does not persuade me. The case rests on conceptual change plus a decisive test, not on support counts.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weak point, and the committee should say so openly. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed HgTe as the platform, and Hasan's photoemission work established the three-dimensional topological insulator. The three-person limit leaves them out, and Pearce is right that the trio is only clean if that exclusion is argued and not assumed. I accept that the committee has argued it only partly. My answer is that Kane and Mele are the conceptual origin and Molenkamp the direct experimental test, so this is the tightest idea-to-observation chain, but it is a judgment and not a proof. Danielsson's Hasan-for-Mele substitution is serious, though I still reject it because Z2 and the quantum spin Hall state were a joint Kane-Mele result. A second weakness is that technological payoff has been slower than early hopes.

responses.point: Pearce supports B059 and says a trio omitting both Hasan and Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang is cleaner only if the exclusion is argued, and rates B059's attribution above B016's.
responses.response: The criticism is fair and I have tried to answer it. The credit is not clean in the sense that Katori and Ye are, and I do not claim it is. My argument is that a prize should follow the logical chain: Kane and Mele conceived the Z2 state, and Molenkamp tested it. Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang chose the material that made the test feasible, which is important but is the step between idea and test, and Hasan's 3D work extends the concept. I would put an explicit sentence in the public description that the three-person limit is not a verdict on them. I agree with you that ease of allocation is a convenience and not merit. That is why I weigh B059 on its science, where I find it strong, and prefer B016 only because the conceptual change in how insulators are classified seems to me larger than a gain in measurement accuracy.

responses.point: Kroll answers my engineering-versus-physics worry: magic-wavelength trapping is an idea about atom-light interaction, the many-body clock work exposes collective effects, and lattice clocks are a different regime from the comb and single-ion prizes.
responses.response: This moves me, in part. Your distinction answers the question Pearce put to the clock supporters: the lattice clock interrogates many neutral atoms at once with the light shift engineered away, which is a difference in kind from single-ion clocks, and a citation naming magic-wavelength trapping would not read as a repeat of 2005 or 2012. I withdraw the suggestion that it is merely engineering. I am not moved on ranking, because I still judge a new classification of electronic matter to be the greater conceptual advance, while your strongest evidence, accuracy near 1e-18, shows a measurement capability. I also accept your point that its attribution is cleaner. I would not oppose B059 as the final prize, and I have moved it to my first alternative.

responses.point: Olsson agrees on the trio and adds that the HgTe quantum spin Hall measurements are demanding and that the broad confirmation lies mostly in 3D materials, so the citation must be limited to the prediction and the HgTe realization.
responses.response: I accept the correction and have changed the citation accordingly, to the prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators and the experimental realization of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe. I would also hold that the independent confirmation I leaned on in round 1 is stronger for the Z2 concept than for the HgTe edge transport itself, and that it comes largely from 3D materials and later 2D platforms. That strengthens the case for crediting the classification as the achievement, with Molenkamp's experiment as its first decisive test. It also makes the Hasan question sharper, and I do not wish to hide that. Your point that the limit belongs to the three-person rule is one I would put in the committee's wording.

responses.point: Danielsson holds that observing correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle graphene is robust and reproduced even though the mechanism is open, that prizes have honoured discoveries before the mechanism was understood, and that B034 has the broadest opening support.
responses.response: This is a fair challenge to my maturity objection. Discoveries have been honoured before their mechanism was settled, and the correlated and superconducting states are reproduced in many laboratories. I now see the maturity worry as a matter of citation wording more than of readiness: a citation limited to the predicted flat bands at the magic angle and the observed correlated and superconducting states would be defensible. I still place B034 behind B016, because its phase diagram is still moving and the experimental credit leaves out Yuan Cao and other first authors, which is a larger omission than in B016. It remains my second alternative, and I would accept it as a final configuration if the committee prefers a more recent discovery with a clean theory-plus-experiment structure.

responses.point: Eriksson moved to B016 from DMFT and notes that the Kane-Mele Z2 invariant is the conceptual foundation on which later work builds, so the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang attribution cuts both ways, and that B034 should not be dismissed on maturity alone.
responses.response: I agree on both points and they sharpen my position. On BHZ, the proposal made the experiment possible but depends on the Z2 framework, so I keep the theory pair intact. On B034, I accept your caution and Danielsson's: maturity alone should not decide. I would add that your wording about topology as a classifying principle of band structure is broader than I want, since it reaches towards the whole field and the 2016 prize. I prefer the narrower citation tied to the quantum spin Hall effect, Z2 and HgTe.

uncertainties: Whether Mele or Hasan should complete the topological insulator trio. I hold Mele, but I recognise that the committee may judge the 3D discovery to have had the larger experimental impact.
How much weight Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang should carry, and whether a citation that states the three-person limit explicitly resolves the fairness concern for the other members.
I have not independently checked the detailed priority chronology for the Z2 proposal and the HgTe experiment.
Whether the committee will see the lattice clock as a distinct discovery or as precision refinement of the 2005 and 2012 lines. I now lean towards distinct, but this does not change my ranking.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My work on complex systems and neural networks does not overlap with the shortlisted topological, clock, circuit or graphene candidates, and the profile documents no connection to any credited name. I note Johansson's disclosure on B013 and Kroll's on B059; neither affects my position on B016.
